issues.legal_issue: A municipal authority may remove unauthorized structures obstructing a public footpath, and the procedural protection required depends on how long the encroachment has been allowed to remain.
material_facts: The occupants had constructed huts on public footpaths and the municipal authority sought to remove them.
The authority had allowed the encroachments to remain for a substantial period and stated that it gave 21 days’ notice before ejectment.
The footpaths were needed for pedestrian passage and traffic movement.
issues.conclusion: The removal power could be exercised, and the action was not contrary to natural justice. A formal personal hearing was not required; where an encroachment has been tolerated for a long time, reasonable notice and an opportunity to remove it voluntarily are required. Notice may be served personally or, if that is not possible for recorded reasons, affixed to the structure with the prescribed witnessing.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 63(i)(19) and 231, read with Section 312(1), empower removal of unauthorized structures on streets and footpaths. Public footpaths are meant for public passage, and no one may use them for a private purpose without authorization. Under Article 21, the procedure for deprivation must be fair and reasonable in the circumstances, but no inflexible hearing requirement applies in every case. Sadan Singh v. New Delhi Municipal Committee recognizes the public’s right of passage and rejects a right to occupy a particular public place for business; Olga Tellis v. Municipal Corporation of Greater Bombay holds that the statutory removal procedure is not unreasonable and that no person has a right to encroach on a footpath or pavement.

predicates.public_footpath_removal_case: A public authority sought to remove an unauthorized structure occupying a public footpath.
predicates.recent_encroachment: The unauthorized occupation had only recently begun when the authority acted.
predicates.long_tolerated_encroachment: The authority had allowed the unauthorized occupation to remain for a substantial period.

issues.definition: When a public authority seeks to remove a footpath encroachment, a formal hearing is unnecessary, but an occupation tolerated for a substantial period requires reasonable notice before removal.

issues.legal_issue: The right to shelter imposes a duty on public authorities to pursue housing provision for poor and indigent people, but does not generally make alternative accommodation a precondition to removing an encroachment from public property.
material_facts: The occupants were described as pavement dwellers and the authority had existing housing and settlement schemes for economically weaker groups.
The proposed alternative sites were outside the immediate area, and the occupants argued that relocation would affect their livelihood.
The authority maintained that the existing sites had basic facilities and that land near the encroachments was not available for housing.
issues.conclusion: The blanket direction requiring accommodation before removal was modified. The Corporation had a constitutional and statutory duty to evolve housing schemes, but alternative accommodation was not, as a general rule, a condition that had to be met before ejectment.
issues.legal_principle: Articles 19(1)(e) and 21 recognize residence and shelter as aspects of fundamental rights; Articles 38, 39 and 46 direct the State to promote welfare and socio-economic justice for weaker sections. Section 284(1) places a statutory housing responsibility on the Corporation in the circumstances it specifies. Article 25(1) of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and Article 11(1) of the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights recognize housing as part of an adequate standard of living. Chameli Singh v. State of U.P. treats the right to shelter as part of Article 21; Shantistar Builders v. Narayan Khimalal Toame recognizes reasonable accommodation as part of the right to life; Olga Tellis v. Municipal Corporation of Greater Bombay addresses the relationship between eviction, livelihood and life; and P.G. Gupta v. State of Gujarat recognizes the State’s duty to make housing accessible to the poor. These rights do not authorize encroachment on public property or create a universal entitlement to alternative accommodation before removal.

predicates.public_encroachment_ejectment_case: A public authority sought to remove poor occupants from an unauthorized occupation of public property.
predicates.poor_occupants_need_shelter: The occupants were poor or indigent people in need of housing.

issues.definition: When a public authority seeks to remove poor occupants from public property, it must pursue housing provision, but need not invariably provide alternative housing before removal.

issues.legal_issue: Benefits under housing schemes for displaced encroachers may be limited to qualifying original occupants and need not be extended to people who acquired the encroachments from them.
material_facts: Some original petitioners had left after accepting money, and other people had taken their places after making payments.
Housing schemes were available subject to eligibility conditions, including an income criterion.
The Court allowed the remaining named original occupants to opt for a scheme if they met its conditions, but excluded later purchasers from the benefits granted to those occupants.
issues.conclusion: The named original occupants could receive an allotment under a scheme if they chose one and satisfied its eligibility criteria. Later occupants who acquired the encroachments by purchase were not entitled to those benefits.
issues.legal_principle: The Court treated transfers of occupation in public encroachments as contrary to constitutional objectives and public policy, stating that such transfers confer no right, title or interest. Housing assistance could be extended under the available schemes according to their eligibility criteria; the Court did not make the same specific direction for later purchasers, to avoid encouraging abuse of the judicial process.

rule.if: public_encroachment_ejectment_case and (original_occupant and scheme_eligibility_met or acquired_encroachment_by_purchase)

predicates.public_encroachment_ejectment_case: A public authority sought to remove occupants from an unauthorized encroachment on public property.
predicates.original_occupant: The occupant was among those originally residing at the encroachment before later occupants took possession.
predicates.scheme_eligibility_met: The occupant satisfied the eligibility conditions of an available housing scheme.
predicates.acquired_encroachment_by_purchase: The occupant paid another person to take over possession of an unauthorized encroachment.

issues.definition: In an encroachment-removal case, scheme benefits may go to original occupants who meet the scheme’s criteria, but not to people who purchased the encroachment.

issues.legal_issue: A court must consider an encroacher’s claim for judicial relief on its merits and cannot reject it solely because the claimant is an encroacher.
material_facts: The occupants sought relief in a constitutional proceeding against removal of their huts.
The municipal authority argued that court intervention would encourage encroachers to abuse the judicial process.
issues.conclusion: The mere fact that encroachers approached the Court was not a ground to dismiss their claims; the Court had to examine whether they had a right to relief and what protection, if any, was appropriate on the facts.
issues.legal_principle: Judicial review is part of the Constitution’s basic structure, and citizens have a right to seek judicial redress for a perceived legal injury. A court must assess the claimant’s asserted right and the facts, while public authorities must assist the court by presenting the relevant factual and legal position. The right of access to court does not itself establish a right to remain on public property.

predicates.judicial_review_case_brought_by_encroach: An occupant of an unauthorized encroachment brought a constitutional proceeding seeking judicial review.
predicates.claimant_seeks_relief_from_removal: The claimant asked the court for protection or other relief against removal of the encroachment.

issues.definition: When an encroacher seeks judicial relief from removal, the court must assess the claim on its merits rather than dismiss it solely because the claimant encroached.

issues.legal_issue: A court may not prescribe a particular budget for housing schemes, but public authorities must plan and pursue housing provision for weaker sections as part of their public responsibilities.
material_facts: The municipal authority described housing schemes already in operation and stated that providing accommodation to every slum dweller exceeded its present means.
A proposal for additional housing was accompanied by an estimated public cost, and the authority referred to constraints on available resources.
issues.conclusion: Courts cannot direct a public authority to implement a scheme with a particular budget because budget-making is an executive function. That limitation does not release the authority from its duty to plan and pursue housing provision for weaker sections, or from using allocations for their designated housing purposes.
issues.legal_principle: Articles 38, 39 and 46 require the State to pursue social and economic justice for weaker sections. Articles 243 to 243ZG establish local bodies as constitutional institutions, and Article 243W concerns their responsibilities for planning and social justice. The Court held that setting a particular annual budget is an executive function, while housing provision and faithful use of designated allocations remain public responsibilities.

predicates.housing_provision_case: A dispute concerns a public authority’s provision of housing for weaker sections.
predicates.public_authority_faces_resource_constrai: The public authority stated that its resources limited the housing it could provide.
predicates.specific_budget_direction_is_sought: A party asked the court to prescribe a particular budget for the housing scheme.

issues.definition: When housing provision is at issue and a public authority faces resource constraints, a court cannot set a particular budget but the authority must still pursue housing provision.
